sections.heading: Gujarat- Museum- Archaeological Museum, Lothal
sections.content: The Archaeological museum at Lothal was set up in 1976 to display the artifacts that were recovered from the excavations conducted from 1952 to 1961 at this site. The museum has three galleries which are treasure houses for beads, terracotta ornaments, replicas of seals, shell and ivory objects, copper and bronze objects, mirrors of bronze and copper, perforated and painted potteries, toy bullock carts and a variety of objects made from stone, shell, and bone and tools and potteries yielded from excavations. The most fabulous are, steatite seals with unicorn motifs and inscription, terracotta seals with elephant motifs, seal, gold necklaces, copper and bronze fish hooks, bangles, perforated jars, painted jars, terracotta bull, horse, model boat, ivory scales and shell compass, chess dices, etc. There are maps and drawings depicting an artists impression of the Harappan town of Lothal. One of the galleries showcases game objects, animal and human figurines, weights, painted potteries, objects recovered from burials and ritual objects, miniature potteries, bricks besides a replica of a joint burial and a scaled plaster of Paris model of the city based on reconstructions made by archeologists.

sections.heading: Gujarat- Monument- Dholavira
sections.content: Proto Historic 3000-2500 BCE Dholavira located on the North West corner of the Khadir Island in Kutch was discovered in the year 1967 and the ruins of the settlement found here are believed to be more than 5000 years old. These excavation sites are one of the largest Harappansites in India. The ruins of the ancient town serve as a proof of the fact that there is a connection with Indus valley because a planned city has been excavated, which is built according to a geometric plan. The city is divided into the citadel, the middle town and the lower town. The excavation brought to light the sophisticated urban planning and architecture, and unearthed large numbers of antiquities. It is estimated that Dholavira is even older than the port city of Lothal as the excavations conducted here came up with a number of ancient artifacts, like seals, beads, animal bones, gold, silver, terracotta ornaments and vessels linked to Mesopotamia. There is even evidence that the town was an important trade center between other settlements in Sind, Punjab and Western Asia. The most fascinating discovery of Dholavira is the large inscription, comprising of ten letters in the Indus script. Each letter has been engraved on slices of crystalline material.

sections.heading: Gujarat- Monument- Step Well- Mata Bhavanis Vav
sections.content: One of the oldest step-wells is the Mata Bhavani's Vav at Ahmedabad, built in the eleventh century. The water is approached by a long flight of steps above which rises a sequence of two, three and four storey open pavilions. The elaborate ornamentation of the columns, brackets and beams and the

sections.heading: Interesting facts
sections.content: Step-wells are one of India's most unique, but little-known, contributions to architecture. The concept of the vav, or stepwell, was a response to the harsh climate of Gujarat and Rajasthan and the acute shortage of water. The practice of making wells into an art form was begun by the Hindus of the Solanki kings but it developed under the Muslim rule. The galleries and chambers surrounding these wells were often carved profusely with elaborate detail and became cool, quiet retreats during the hot summers.

sections.heading: Rani ki Vav- Patan
sections.content: The Rani Vav at Patan, was built during the late eleventh century, by the Queen Udaymati after the death of her husband, King Bhimdeva I of the Solanki dynasty. A massive structure of seven storeys, it is probably the most magnificent step-well in Gujarat. Multi-storey colonnades and retaining walls link a stepped tank to a deep circular well. Throughout, there is a rich ornamentation. Columns, brackets and beams are encrusted with scrollwork and the wall niches are carved with figures. The designs on walls and pillars include, leaves, flowers, birds, fish and other breathtaking ornamental designs. At water level the figure of Vishnu on Seshanaga and the Buddha is included among the Dasavataras, the ten incarnations of Lord Vishnu.

sections.heading: Gujarat- Monument- Step Well- Ruda Baoli- Adalaj
sections.content: One of the well preserved and intricately sculpted step well is the Ruda baoli at Adalaj, located 12 miles north of Ahmedabad. Octagonal in shape, it has stairways from three sides meeting on a wide landing from where it descends down to the water level. The long flight of steps descend, columns and connecting beams create open structures of increasing complexity; the receding perspectives of columns and cross-beams are particularly striking. Wall niches incorporate miniature pilasters, eaves and roof-like pediments. The decoration of the columns, curved brackets and lintels is highly elaborate with repeated friezes and ornamentation of animal motifs and deities. Ahmedabad in Gujarat, has a rich historical heritage that can be traced back to the ancient times. The city was built in 1411 by Sultan Ahmad Shah. Humayun took over Gujarat in 1534 then lost it and it was reclaimed by Akbar in 1572 and therefore has a legacy of Indo- Islamic architecture. The city was surrounded by walls that still exist.

sections.heading: Gujarat- Monument- Mosque- Siddi Bashir Mosque (Shaking Minarets) - Ahmedabad
sections.content: Known as Shaking Minaret or Jhulta Minar, this small mosque was constructed by Ahmed Shah II for his mother. When one minaret is shaken the other one begins to vibrate. The vibrations at the base of the tower multiply and get transmitted through air tunnels between the two towers. Amazingly, the connecting passageway between the two minarets, however, remains free of any vibration! It was in the nineteenth century, Monier M Williams, a European Sanskrit scholar who first noticed the minarets shaking. Each minaret is three storied tall with delicately carved stone balconies around each storey. Ahmedabad has many such examples of shaking minarets. The mosque at Raj Bibi once had a pair of shaking minarets. But the British, who were ruling over India at that time, dismantled one minaret in order to study the secret of its construction and the mystery behind the swinging effect. The other such shaking minarets are at the mosques of Jami-Masjid and Bibi-ki-Masjid. Sidi Bashir's minars are all that remain of the mosque popularly named after one of Ahmed Shah's favourite slaves. These are the best existing examples of the shaking minarets- built on a foundation of flexible sandstone.

sections.heading: Gujarat- Monument- Mosque- Jami Masjid- Ahmedabad
sections.content: The largest mosque in Ahmedabad built by Sultan Ahmed Shah I, the founder of Ahmedabad was Jami Masjid. Built in 1424, it is considered as one of the most superb and imposing structures of its class in the world. It is a massive structure with entrances on three sides- west, south and north. The eastern porches have the mausoleum of Sultan Ahmed Shah I. The mosque, which stands on 260 pillars, is supported by 15 domes arranged symmetrically. A feature of the mosque is the royal gallery with beautiful stonework. The courtyard is surrounded by an enclosed corridor. The mosque shows distinctive blend of Hindu and Jain influence on the Sultanate period architecture. Sculptures on the dome and jalis are the evidence that traditional Hindu craftsmen and architects built it while the columns in the hall within the mosque are in Arabic style.

sections.heading: Gujarat- Monument- Step Well- Dada Harirs Vav- Ahmedabad
sections.content: The Dada Harir's vav at Ahmedabad, is one of the finest example of the Mughal period. The Dada Harir's vav is modelled on the earlier Mata Bhavani's vav, though it has an additional domed pavilion at the entrance. One striking feature of this vav is the complete absence of figural themes. The motifs in stylized scrollwork that adorn the wall niches are examples of Islamic architecture.

sections.heading: Surya Temple,Modhera
sections.content: A masterpiece of the Solanki dynasty, the Sun Temple at Modhera is one of the few shrines that are dedicated to the Sun God apart from the one at Konark and Martand. Situated on the banks of Pushpavati river, it was built by King Bhimdev (believed to be the descendant of the lineage of Sun God). The temple has a shrine that is designed in a manner, so that the first rays of the Sun shine on the image of the Lord Surya in the garbhagriha. Though the Temple was plundered by Mahmud Ghazni; the architectural grandeur has still not vanished. Erected on a high platform, the Temple appears majestic with its grand structure and the Toranas leading to the main halls. The exterior walls are engraved with intricate carvings, and every single inch of the structure is covered with the sculptural patterns of Gods, Goddesses, birds, beasts and flowers. The Sun Temple is divided into three parts namely Surya Kund, Sabha Mandap and Guda Mandap. Surya Kund is a deep stepped tank in the front of the temple that was used to store pure water. The devotees used to take a halt here for ceremonial purposes before moving towards the temple. More than 108 shrines mark the steps of this tank including the shrines dedicated to Lord Ganesha, Lord Shiva, Sheetala Mata and many others. In front of the tank, a huge torana (archway) leads to the Sabha Mandap. Sabha Mandapwas the assembly hall where religious gatherings took place. This hall is open from all the four sides and has 52 delicately carved pillars. The intricate carvings depict scenes from the Ramayana, Mahabharata and scenes from the life of Lord Krishna. In order to get into the garbhagriha, one has to cross the passage with pillars and arches. Guda Mandap is the garbhagriha that is supported by a lotus-base plinth. Once, this hall used to house the idol of the Sun God. The designing of the hall was done in a way, so that the idol gets the first glimpse of the Sun at equinoxes. The walls represent the Sun God in his 12 different facets of each month. The carved walls also depict the aspects of human life like the cycle of birth and death.

sections.heading: Gujarat- Monument- Jain Temples  Palitana
sections.content: Palitana temples are considered to be the most sacred amongst all the Jain temples and perhaps the largest cluster of Jain temples anywhere. From the base to the peak of the Shatrunjaya hill, where the temples are located, there are in all 863 temples. The interesting fact is that no one is allowed to sleep overnight including the priest, because the temple city has been built as an abode for the Gods. The temples dedicated to the Jain Tirthankaras were built in two phases-the eleventh and twelfth centuries in the first phase and in the sixteenth century as the second phase. Some of the earliest temples built in the eleventh century were destroyed by Muslim invaders in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. The current temples date back to sixteenth century onwards. The hilltops are bounded by sturdy walls and the temples are grouped into nine enclosures each having several minor temples clustered around a central temple. Like the Jains who prefer the purity of white, their temples too are usually white, a combination of plaster and marble. The temples are elaborately ornamental. Throughout the cluster one can see detailed carvings, beautiful idols and images, jeweled statues and intricate toranas. Among the most important temples here, is the Chaumukh temple with its four-faced deity of Adinath enshrined on a marble pedestal in a shrine open on all four sides. Built in the early seventeenth century, it is planned as a large square subdivided into smaller squares, each structure topped by a dome. The innermost five domes topped squares form a cross and represent the five hills sacred to the Jains. The Adishwar temple is probably the most profusely decorated in Palitana. Its ornate pillars and roofs are decorated with intricately cut marble in the shape of dragons. Near the Adishwar temple is the Muslim shrine of Angar Pir. Childless couples make offerings of miniature cradles at this shrine in the hope of being blessed with children. Other temples worth mentioning are the Sampriti Raj, Kumarpal, and Rampal temples.

sections.heading: Calico Museum collection
sections.content: One of the finest textile museums in the world it is housed in a carved wooden haveli. Located in the Sarabhai Foundation, in Shahibagh the Calico Museum of Textiles, was constructed in 1949. Along with the finest collection of not just textiles and clothes the museum boasts of furniture, temple artifacts and crafts of the country. It has a collection of the finest fabrics spun, woven, printed and painted in different parts of India during the last five centuries. One can see the exquisite designs and artwork in kalamkaris, pichhwais, patolas, bandhnis, floor spreads, tent canopies and precious brocades.It has a collection of marble, sandstone and bronze icons and busts split in two thematic sections- gallery for religious textiles and historical textiles. There are colourful embroidered wall hangings depicting legends of Krishna, cloth decorated with tie and dye, glinting mirror work, screen prints, block prints and intricate embroidery. There is an embroidered tent and the robes of Shah Jahan, along with elaborate carpets and plump cushions that once furnished Muslim palace. Special exhibits include Kashmiri shawls, Kullu embroidery, glittering silk brocades from Varanasi, folk art from the Punjab and masks and large wooden temple rathas from Tamil Nadu. The collection also includes some of the best examples of the Patola saris woven in Patan as well as the extravagant Zari work that gilds saris in heavy gold stitching which weigh almost nine kilos.

sections.heading: Vechaar Utensils Museum
sections.content: is a unique museum located on the outskirts of Ahmedabad city. Established in 1981, this museum exhibits utensils of all shapes and sizes. The exhibits have been collected from all over the country and have been displayed around a simple courtyard. The collection includes pots used for storing water cooking and serving utensils, spoons, rolling pins, tiffin carriers, vessel for churning buttermilk, storage jars, feeding cups for infants and havan kunds too. The collection includes pottery, terracotta and wooden articles as well. The display gives a glimpse into the lifestyle of people of the place they belong to and also the craftsmanship involved.

sections.heading: Kite Museum
sections.content: Museum situated in Sanskar Kendra the museum was established in 1985 having a fabulous collection of kites from all over the world. There are artistic kites, rare kites that have been crafted from more than 400 pieces of paper. It is the second such museum in the world. Bhanubhai Shah, a conoisseur of kites is the brain behind the concept of the museum and he is responsible for designing and donating kites to the museum. garba dances, mirror work and block prints,the kites are of different styles. The kites are made from different materials as well. The materials include paper, cloth, polythene, and nylon. One of the most lavishly designed and decorated kites are the hexagonal Rokoku - beautiful Japanese kites.

sections.heading: Gujarat- Museum- Shreyas Folk Museum  Ahemadabad
sections.content: A really informative and educational museum located close to the suburbs of Ambavadi near Sabarmati is the Shreyas Folk Museum. This museum displays the colorful and traditional folk arts of Gujarat. From textile and clothing to the decorative crafts, the Shreyas Folk Museum brings out the traditional rustic flavor and cultural heritage of Gujarat. The Museum has an exclusive collection of folk arts and objects which reflect the colorful and traditional heritage of Gujarat and gives an insight into the traditional crafts and technology. The collections reflect many of the traditional and rural communities. These communities belong to different villages of Gujarat and in this museum one can get a glimpse of their exquisite artwork. The communities whose culture and folk art are being researched here are Kathi, Rabari, Rharan, Ahir, Brahmins, Banias, Meghvals, Bharvad, Kanbi, Koli, Mer, Bhansali, Rajputs, Khojas, Vohras, Memons and the Miyanas. One of the unique attractions is a complete skeleton of an elephant which has a height of 3.19m. There is an extensive collection of old coins, weapons, puppets, toys, costumes, masks, musical fountains and animal caparisons which recall the grandeur of the bygone era and projects a vintage charm.

sections.heading: Gujarat- Museum- The NC Mehta Gallery  Ahmedabad
sections.content: Designed by the famous architect Le Corbusier, the NC Mehta Gallery is one of the museums in Ahmedabad which houses an exclusive range of miniature paintings collected from various parts of India, these miniature paintings are the collections of Late Shri Nanalal C. Mehta who was one of the pioneers of Indian miniature painting and the NC Mehta Gallery, Ahmedabad was named after him. He published several books on Sanskrit and Hindi literature and discovered new documents on Indian paintings. Vasanta Vilasa scroll and Chaurapanchasika are some of the treasured collections apart from miniature paintings that include sacred works, ragmala paintings, royal portraits and different social scenes. The Gallery has examples of Western India and Sultanate School paintings, folios of the Jain Kalpasutra and also the Pre-Mughal style folios. One can see folios of the Hamza-Nama and the Sikander Nama which are two of the famous Persian epics. These miniature paintings were mostly drawn on handmade paper with mineral colors. The aim of the display is to inculcate the love for art and paintings in our society and also for the research and further studies in art work.

sections.heading: The basic and foremost feature of this unique form of painting is an exhaustive detailing of each and every component relating to the scene.
sections.content: There are four primary schools of Indian Miniature Paintings - the Rajput, the Mughal, Pahari and the Deccan schools. Miniature Painters used varied substances for coloring their drawings, namely- minerals, vegetables, precious stones, indigo, conch shells, pure gold and silver. The illustrated manuscripts of Jains and Buddhists, and the flowering of the Mughal, Rajput, Pahari and Deccan Miniatures are noted for their meticulous execution and artistic skills. The fine stroke of brushes conveyed the themes from the Ramayana, Mahabharata, Bhagvata Purana, Rasikpriya, Rasamanjiri, etc. The themes have also emerged from the compositions of the great poets like Sur, Keshav, Bihari, Matiram, Dev and Puhukar who wrote great poems like Sursagar, Bihari Satsai, Rasraj, Ashtayam and Rasbeli. There are several themes of different nature. They centered on the love of Radha and Krishna. definite narrative content. These brilliantly illustrated paintings glow as if illuminated from inside. The use of bold contrasts such as red, green, blue yellow is definitely a native influence. Artists belonging to Pahari school of painting used bright colors and depicted themes of love. These Paintings from the Hills, were developed at the Hindu royal courts of Kulu, Guler, Mankot, Nurpur, Mandi, Kangra and Basoholi regions of the North Indian mountain valleys.

sections.heading: Gujarat- Museum- Junagarh
sections.content: An ancient fortified city rich in myth and legend, Junagadh has beautiful shrines of Hindus, Jains and Muslims. Deriving its name from the 'old fort', which circles this medieval town, Junagadh was the capital of the Kshattrapa dynasty. The Girnar Hills that landscape Junagadh are a holy refuge to the Jains. The history of Mount Girnar dates back to the empire of Ashoka, who inscribed 14 edicts on a huge boulder en-route to Mt. Girnar peak. There is a huge boulder, housed in a small roadside building, on which are fourteen rock edicts inscribed by Emperor Ashoka.

sections.heading: Cave Temples
sections.content: There are three main caves which were probably Jain and Buddhist monasteries. Babapyara cave is Jain while the cave in Uparkot Fort and the Kapurkodiya caves are Buddhist. Since they were used for residential purposes of the monks they are very plain and have simple and few carvings. Only the Uparkot cave has ancient carvings on its walls and pillars.

sections.heading: Lakshmi Vilas Palace
sections.content: is an extravagant building built by Maharaja Sayajirao Gaekwad III in 1890. Right from its imposing façade to its ornate interiors, Laxmi Vilas Palace, Vadodara, is the palace which still serves as the residence of the Gaekwad family. The interiors of the palace radiate opulence and are styled with marble mosaic, fine stone and elegant furnishings. Having a Venetian mosaic floor, Belgian stained glass windows and walls with intricate mosaic decorations, the palace features a grand Durbar Hall which is sometimes the venue of music concerts and other cultural events.. Outside of the Darbar Hall is an Italian courtyard of water fountains. The walls of the Durbar Hall are beautified with brilliant mosaic decorations. There is a commendable collection of old armory,

sections.heading: Vadodara- Museum- Maharaja Fateh Singh Museum
sections.content: Maharaja Fateh Singh Museum is a museum situated in a corner of the 750-acre grounds of the Lakshmi Vilas Palace built by Sayajirao III, the highly progressive ruler of the former princely state of Baroda. This used to be the royal school for the children of the family. The works of art belonging to the Royal family are displayed in the museum. The major works of art in this museum are the paintings by European and Indian artists including a collection of the commissioned paintings by Raja Ravi Varma. The collection includes portraits of the Royal family in addition to the paintings based on Hindu mythology for which Raja Ravi Varma was famous. There is a collection of sculptures in marble and bronze. These include copies of great masters in bronze commissioned by the royal family of Baroda. This includes original works of renowned artists like Fellicci, an Italian artist whose works adorn not only the Museum but also the Lakshmi Vilas Palace. Some of Fellici's works can be seen in the Public Park known as Sayaji Garden. The museum has an oriental gallery which houses Japanese and Chinese sculptures, Korean ceramics, Japanese screens, copies of Renaissance masterpieces etc. These works were mainly collected by Maharaja Sayajirao Gaekwad during his visits abroad.

sections.heading: Raja Ravi Verma & his paintings
sections.content: Raja Ravi Varma was born on April 29, 1848 at Kilimanoor, a small town in Kerala. His uncle was a well known artist known as Raja Raja Varma who gave him elementary art lessons. He was taken to Thiruvananthapuram in his fourteenth year to stay in the royal palace and learn oil painting. Ravi Varma had many opportunities to discover and learn new techniques and media in the field of painting. His later years spent in Mysore, Baroda and other parts of the country enabled him to sharpen and expand his skills and blossom into a mature and complete painter. He was the first artist to cast the Indian Gods and mythological characters in natural earthy surroundings using European realism. His dazzling oil paintings of Indias ancient glory and his mass reproductions through oleography reached out to the Indian populace in an extraordinary scale at the turn of the twentieth Century. Varma had already made a name for himself as a highly talented painter who had mastered the European painter, the Odore Jensen at the Travancore court. His technique of oil painting observing a visiting Dutch paintings had won prizes at Madras and had been highly appreciated by the British governor too. But Baroda, definitely, was a major turning point in his career. Varma was invited to paint a portrait of the 18-year-old Sayajirao Gaekwad in 1881. The young prince was so happy with the result that he not only commissioned Varma to paint portraits of many of his family members thereafter, but also got him to execute more artistically ambitious works on themes drawn from Puranic legends, Sanskrit classics and mythological epics to decorate the newly built Lakshmi Vilas palace. Varma, was one of the first Indian artist to adopt the style of French and British naturalist painters by adopting devices like the chiaroscuro and dramatic lighting effects in the oil-on-canvas medium. But Varma employed these western techniques to paint purely Indian themes. Episodes from literary and mythological sources like those of Dushyant-Shakuntala, Nala-Damayanti, Radha-Krishna, Harishchandra-Taramati, the Mahabharata and the Ramayana were his favourite subjects.

sections.heading: Gujarat- Handicrafts- Sankheda Laquerware Furniture
sections.content: Sankheda in Gujarat is famous for artistic furniture of low seats, tables, stools and Jhoola. The lacquerware is found designed into chair-backs and chair-legs, hand-rests, and specially carved shapes to make the chairs more attractive. The colours used for lacquering are gold, silver, red, blue, yellow, orange and black. The lacquerware itself has designs using the above colour combinations as dots, squares, and other geometric or floral motifs.

sections.heading: Embroidery
sections.content: is an integral part of life in Gujarat from superbly embroidered toranas to chaklas or wall hangings, beautifully embroidered dresses like lehngas, cholis and dupattas, mens kurtas, churidhars, childrens clothes and so on. Aribharat or hook embroidery, mochibarat, rabari, banni and soof embroidery and applique work are among the many beautiful embroideries of this state. Abhala is the embroidery where small round pieces of mirrors are fixed on to the fabric using buttonhole stitching; the embroidery is done in a herringbone stitch using silken thread. Rust, light green, indigo, blue, deep red, pink, and purple are the colours used. Kathi is the oldest embroidery which is known for its romantic motifs. Geometrical motifs are fabricated with multicolored fabric pieces leading to patch work effect. Varieties of items are prepared. Heer is an embossed stitch having shades of off-white, yellow, madder red, black, indigo, ivory, and green. Small mirror pieces are used to add more beauty to the embroidery. Ari embroidery with silk threads using a hook is a popular craft of Kutch. The motifs found commonly are, dancing peacocks, human figures in dancing poses etc. A Bandhani pattern with beautiful and delicate bead work is unique. The various communities in Gujarat, rabaris, ahirs, jats, bharwads have their own styles of embroidery. The embroidery of the Rabari community is usually done on a maroon background with the enclosed motifs. A style of embroidery in Saurashtra known as mahajan has a special design called kajuri in which a satin shine and fine effects are attained by special manipulation of the satin and herringbone stitches with interplay of glowing red and shades of violet. Applique is an integral part of the decorative needlework of Gujarat with its own distinctive style. It is done on patchwork in which pieces of coloured and patterned fabrics are finely cut in different shapes and sizes and then sewn together on a plain background to form a composite piece. Saurashtra and Kutch are also noted for their bead work whose designs lean heavily on the embroidery and the bandhini patterns. A whole gamut of articles are made of beads like decorations for domestic animals, cradles, coverlets, hangings, toranas, purses, little perches that sit on a woman's head to balance water pots, fans and a whole range of ornamental pieces for the house.

sections.heading: Pottery
sections.content: Kutch and Saurashtra in Gujarat are noted for their beautiful earthenware. They produce natural white wares in attractive shapes and designs. Banaskantha produces water pots that are very artistically and skilfully decorated. Vidi, a small village in Kutch is abundant in white clay for manufacturing this

sections.heading: Gujarat- Handicrafts -Wood Carvings
sections.content: Gujarat is one of the richest regions known for wood carvings. Even the ordinary houses of this state are beautifully decorated with carvings. A fascinating feature of Gujarat carvings is the large variations found in a single motif. Currently, both old Indian style carved furniture with low seats and tables, as well as modern furnitures are produced. In the traditional style, well known items are: nav khania and tran khania, cupboards with nine and three compartments for keeping personal belongings, the paniara stands for water pots which need special mention because of their very lovely carvings, mostly floral and geometrical and the jhula (swing). Pethapur in Mehsana district is famous for engraving of blocks for textile printing for which teakwood is mostly used.

sections.heading: Gujarat- Handicrafts- Silks
sections.content: Gujarat has developed its own style of kinkhabs (brocades) woven with extra weft patterns. At one time these were exported to as far as Russian royalty from the port of Surat. Kanbis or patidars, khatris and mommin (particularly the women) are expert craftspersons in this field. There are dozens of designs in vogue like tara mandal- a rather complicated constellation, animals, fruits, stylised dance figures, peacocks, women waving fans and lotus flowers in many shapes. Rudrol in Mehsana district, Jamnagar and Dokla produce them. Several varieties of silk like gajji and mashru are made. A famous item is the Nathdwara pichwai in brochade style. Tanchoi fabric iswoven in Surat. In tanchoi sarees the designs are always floral with interspersing of birds. The usual ground is bright blue, purple, green or red with areas patterned in tabby weave. Figures of flying birds, paired cocks amidst floral sprays are worked on them. Sometimes the pallu is done more solidly with peacocks, baskets or bunches of flowers or hunting scenes. Patola is the most colourful and elaborate weave with its figured body and the subtle merging of one shade into another. The most renowned amongst patolas is the one made in Patan in Mehsana district. These patolas comprise mostly of the wedding saree with dark green, white or yellow against a ruby red background, and leaf and flower patterns while the pallu features dancing girls and parrots or swans.

sections.heading: Gujarat- Handicrafts- Bandhani Craft
sections.content: Bandhani, the craft of tie and dye of fabrics is an ancient art practiced in many places in Gujarat and Rajasthan. Jamnagar, Anjar and Bhuj are famous centres of this form of craft. Bandhanis of each of these regions are distinctive in design, technique, and ornamentation. The cloth is folded and dyed and designs are created with the combination of small dots and circles. The borders are broad and are worked both in matching and contrasting colours. Amongst the numerous designs the two important ones are barah bagh or bavan bagh which means twelve gardens or fifty two gardens. It is said that the entire bandhani tradition of this region is manifested in the gharchola, a form of a saree. The making of the gharchola is a complicated and time-consuming process. A starched silk odhni or sari is fixed to a large wooden frame using nails. The sari/odhini, coloured red or green, is divided into a network of squares by rows of white tie-dyed spots or woven bands of zari. Motifs within each compartment range from elephants, parrots, and flowers to dancing girls. Jamnagar has a satiny, silk type of glazed silk on which bandhani is done for blouses, vests and lamp shades.

sections.heading: Gujarat- Handicrafts -Crochet Lacework
sections.content: The oldest centre of crochet lace work in Gujarat is Jamnagar where the women of the Vohra community have been engaged in this art since Aurangzeb's time. They specialize in a particular type of conical cap that is shaped using a mould of conical shape while crocheting. The colours are dark, black and brown with white and look as effective as ikat work.

sections.heading: Garba Dance
sections.content: Navaratri or nine nights before Dussera is the most colourful festival of Gujarat when worship of the mother goddess and her numerous forms takes place in October. During the celebration which starts in the evening and continues till late at night, people assemble together in squares and temple compounds and sing and dance. Garba dance is performed in a circle by men and women around an earthenware pot called a garbo, filled with water. As the dancers whirl around the pot, a singer and a drummer provide the musical accompaniment. The participants clap in a steady rhythm. At times they dance with small and colourful sticks on rhythm and instead of clapping use sticks held in both hands. This is known as dandia. As they whirl to the rhythm of the dance, men and women strike the dandias together, adding to the joyous atmosphere. Proto historic 2500-600 BCE The 4,500-year-old archaeological site of Lothal belonging to the Indus Valley Civilisation was discovered in 1954. Like the cities of Mohenjodaro and Harappa in Pakistan, Lothal too had excellent architecture and town planning. Lothal is prominent as the walled city and as the port from where overseas trade was conducted. The dwellings were constructed with baked bricks and had underground drains as in Mohenjodaro. Lothal, literally means 'the mound of the dead, and the most architecturallysophisticated part is its dockyard, which provided berthing facilities for the ships. Constructed from kiln-baked bricks, the dock comprised a basin. A wide channel was constructed to facilitate entry of ships. Near the dock were warehouses for storage of cargo brought in by the ships. This was probably one of the most important ports on the subcontinent. Lothal was an active business center and had business links with Mesopotamia, Egypt and Persia as the seals discovered at the site suggest. The entire city had a drainage system, well laid-out, paved roads and a bath for every house, some of which were double storied and built on mud platforms. Beads made in the city were quite famous and there is evidence of a bead factory in Lothal. Pottery was another flourishing industry. The ruins of a fire altar suggest that the people of Lothal worshipped the fire god along with the sea god. The unique Harappan system of weights and measures was used in Lothal too. Bricks were in a perfect ratio and the decimal system was used for measuring width.
